title: Reproducible development, APIs and delivery
summary: Move Cinderline's scrap job from a notebook to one reviewed commit: five delivery states with their evidence, a tested package, a bundle with dev, test and prod targets, the CLI, SDK and REST as one API, and authentication that keeps tokens out of code.
objectives: Name the five delivery states of a change and the evidence that proves each one.
Lay out a package with unit tests and a bundle with dev, test and prod targets, and predict what each target resolves to.
Classify checks as local or authenticated, choose the CLI, SDK or REST for a task, authenticate people and pipelines correctly, and write a promotion checklist ticked only by evidence.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
Five states, five kinds of evidence
Branches, pull requests and Git folders
A package, its tests and its pins
The CLI, the SDK and REST
Who authenticates, and where the credential lives
Gates from pull request to prod

questions.prompt: A status report says the scrap change is 'done: validate printed Validation OK! for prod and the wheel built'. Which delivery state has actually been reached?

options.text: Validation: the configuration resolves for prod under an identity; nothing is deployed or run.
options.rationale: Right: validate authenticates and resolves the target but uploads nothing and starts no run; deployment and execution still need their own evidence.

options.text: Deployment: a built wheel means the job exists in prod.
options.rationale: Building a wheel is a local artifact step; only bundle deploy creates or updates the job and records state.

options.text: Execution: Validation OK! means the job ran successfully.
options.rationale: Execution evidence is a run ID with a result state; validate never starts a run.

options.text: Reviewed artifact: a clean validate is the approval.
options.rationale: Review is a person reading the diff and the plan; the CLI cannot approve a change.

questions.prompt: A pull request moves `catalog: cinderline_prod` into the test target's variables. Unit tests pass and `validate --strict --target test` prints Validation OK!. What should the reviewer conclude?

options.text: Reject it: test would read and write production data; validate checks structure and resolution, not whether a value is the right one for the environment.
options.rationale: Right: a legal, resolvable value can still be wrong; only a reviewer reading databricks.yml as code catches a target pointed at another environment's data.

options.text: Approve it: validate passed, so the configuration is correct for test.
options.rationale: Validate proves the configuration resolves for an identity and target; it has no idea which catalog test is supposed to use.

options.text: Approve it: unit tests cover the catalog name.
options.rationale: Unit tests exercise pure functions on records; the catalog name is a parameter they never see.

options.text: Reject it because a target may not assign a variable.
options.rationale: Targets may assign declared variables; that is how catalog differs per environment.

questions.prompt: Which arrangement lets the CI runner deploy to prod as the prod service principal with no Databricks secret stored anywhere in CI?

options.text: Workload identity federation: the runner presents its CI platform's own token, which is exchanged for a Databricks token for the principal.
options.rationale: Right: the federated auth type needs only the host and client ID; the CI platform's token is exchanged and nothing Databricks-specific is stored.

options.text: OAuth machine-to-machine with the client secret in the CI secret store.
options.rationale: That works and is the fallback, but it stores a Databricks secret (the client secret) in CI.

options.text: A personal access token of the prod service principal in an environment variable.
options.rationale: A stored token is exactly the secret the question excludes, and tokens should not be the pipeline's method.

options.text: Running databricks auth login once on the runner and keeping its profile.
options.rationale: That is a person's browser login; deployments would act as that person, and the cached token is a stored credential.

cards.prompt: What does a green unit-test run prove about the scrap job in prod?
cards.answer: Only the local source state: validation, deployment and execution each still need their own evidence.
cards.explanation: Unit tests run functions on a laptop without a workspace, so they cannot see a missing root path, a wrong identity or a job that never ran. Validation is proven by a validate summary naming host and user, deployment by a deploy log and state, execution by a run ID with a result state. A status sentence should name the state reached and stop there.

cards.prompt: Why tie the prod target to git.branch main?
cards.answer: So the CLI refuses to plan or deploy prod from any other branch unless --force is given, keeping prod on reviewed commits.
cards.explanation: When bundle.git.branch is set and the checkout is on another branch, plan and deploy stop with 'not on the right Git branch'. Combined with a pull request that requires review and passing checks before main moves, prod can only be deployed from commits that went through both. The escape hatch, --force, belongs in no pipeline script.

cards.prompt: Which parts of the scrap project run without a workspace, and why?
cards.answer: The rules in scrap.py and the parameter parser: pure functions with records in and rows out, no Spark, files or network.
cards.explanation: Dividing code by what it needs makes the rules testable anywhere: scrap.py takes records and returns rows, params.py parses and validates arguments. Only the thin entry point touches the platform, reading an export from a volume and writing a summary, and even it runs on a temporary folder in the lab. The deployed code is exactly the tested code, and a reviewer reads a short diff instead of a notebook export.

cards.prompt: Why is 1 scrapped of 32 inspected a good unit-test case?
cards.answer: It is exactly 0.03125, a tie at the fifth decimal that separates the half-up rule (0.0313) from Python's round (0.0312).
cards.explanation: Good cases separate a right rule from a nearly right one: a tie exposes the rounding rule, an idle line exposes whether no rate is confused with zero, a rate exactly at the threshold exposes 'above' versus 'at or above', and a record with more scrapped than inspected exposes rejection. The expected values are worked out by hand before the code runs; a value copied from the code's own output proves nothing.

cards.prompt: Which values belong in per-target variables, and which must stay identical everywhere?
cards.answer: Where data lives and which workspace and identity act (catalog, schema, host, run_as) vary per target; business rules such as the alert threshold stay identical.
cards.explanation: Variables are declared once in databricks.yml and assigned per target, so the code receives --catalog cinderline_test in test and cinderline_prod in prod without knowing which environment it is in. A business rule overridden in one target means the two environments run different logic, and a passing test run stops being evidence about prod. Secrets belong in neither: they come from the environment or a secret scope.

cards.prompt: The commit did not change but Friday's build fails where Monday's passed; what do you check first?
cards.answer: What the build resolved: an unpinned requirement such as pyyaml>=6 lets each build pick a different release.
cards.explanation: Two builds of one commit should be the same software. A version range turns every build into an unannounced upgrade, so when the only difference between a passing and a failing build is the date, suspect dependency resolution first. Pin libraries, build tools, the CLI and the SDK to exact versions, record the resolved versions with the build's evidence, and upgrade a pin in its own pull request so the effect is isolated.

cards.prompt: What happens when the include pattern is mistyped as resource/*.yml?
cards.answer: The wildcard matches no file, the CLI raises no error for an empty wildcard, and the bundle deploys without its job.
cards.explanation: Only the root databricks.yml's include is processed. In CLI v1.17.0 an include entry without wildcards that matches nothing is an error, but a wildcard that matches nothing produces no message, so the job file is silently never loaded and a deploy succeeds with nothing in it. Check the resources you expect with databricks bundle summary after a deploy, and let a local structure rule refuse an include that matches no file.

cards.prompt: What does mode: production require that mode: development does not?
cards.answer: An explicit workspace.root_path, so only one copy of the deployment exists; development instead makes private, prefixed, paused copies per person.
cards.explanation: Development mode sets presets: a [dev <short name>] prefix, a dev tag, paused schedules and triggers, four concurrent runs, and a default root path in the deployer's home folder, so two developers get two private copies. Production mode sets no presets but checks that one copy exists: a missing root_path is an error, softened to a recommendation when every job sets run_as or a service principal deploys.

cards.prompt: Which result can come only from databricks bundle validate, never from a local check?
cards.answer: A summary naming the workspace user the configuration was resolved for, because validate's initialize phase asks the workspace who the current user is.
cards.explanation: A YAML parse proves the text is YAML; local structure rules prove the files have the shape a team requires. Validate connects to the workspace, reads the current user, resolves variables and paths, applies the full schema and mode rules and prints host, user and path before Validation OK!. If a pipeline log shows a person's name on the User line, the pipeline is not authenticating as its service principal.

cards.prompt: What can the team claim after databricks bundle deploy --target test succeeds?
cards.answer: That the job and its files exist in test as configured and deployment state was recorded; the job has not run.
cards.explanation: Deploy takes the lock, uploads the wheel and synchronized files, applies the plan and records state, and starts no run. Execution evidence is a run ID with a result state from bundle run or the schedule, and correctness needs that run's output compared with an expectation. Prod is separate evidence again: its own root path, identity, permissions and branch rule.

cards.prompt: When is the SDK the better choice than the CLI or a raw REST call for starting a run?
cards.answer: From Python automation that needs authentication, safe retries and a waiter, such as a service that starts a run when a file lands.
cards.explanation: All three end in POST /api/2.2/jobs/run-now. The SDK adds typed arguments, the default authentication chain, retries for failures that are safe to retry and a waiter; the CLI adds commands, profiles and bundles and suits people and deployment pipelines; raw REST suits a language without an SDK or a case needing the exact request. Whichever client, the workspace receives one identical request under the caller's identity.

cards.prompt: How should a CI pipeline authenticate to deploy prod?
cards.answer: As the prod service principal, through OAuth machine-to-machine with the secret injected from the CI store or through workload identity federation with no stored secret.
cards.explanation: A person's browser login (OAuth user-to-machine) is right for a laptop and wrong for prod: deployments would act as that person and break when they leave. A service principal acts under its own permissions; M2M needs a client ID and secret from the CI secret store, federation exchanges the CI platform's own token and stores nothing. Neither writes a credential into code or databricks.yml, whose workspace section has no token field.

cards.prompt: Which checks run on a pull request, and which run only after a merge?
cards.answer: Pull request: unit tests, local checks and validate --strict for test. Merge: deploy to test, run the job and check its output. Prod follows an approval.
cards.explanation: Continuous integration runs the cheap, workspace-free checks and one authenticated validate on every proposed change so nothing unreviewed reaches main. Continuous delivery acts only on merged commits: deploy and run in test as the test service principal, then, after a second person reviews the prod plan, deploy the same commit to prod as the prod principal. Each gate records the commit SHA, the CLI version and its identity, and a failing gate stops the line.

cards.prompt: What does a promotion move, and when may a checklist row be ticked?
cards.answer: One reviewed commit, deployed to the next environment with that environment's own configuration; a row is ticked only by its own evidence.
cards.explanation: Copying notebooks between workspaces ties nothing to a review; rebuilding the same commit with pinned tools gives the same software. Each row names its evidence: the approval, test counts at the SHA, the validate summary, the reviewed plan, the test run's ID and output check, the prod deploy log with the same SHA. A successful deploy is not a successful run, so a neighbouring row's evidence never ticks another.
